fatal_errors: Cold work cannot readily vary heterogeneous lattice strain while holding dislocation density, texture, and other deformation structures constant; intermediate annealing intended to equalize those variables would also relax the proposed strain mediator.
The hypothesis conflates intrinsic, composition-dependent atomic lattice distortion with residual heterogeneous strain introduced by plastic deformation.
The cited evidence does not establish a roughly 20% strengthening threshold for cold-work-induced lattice strain in equiatomic FeCoCrNiMn.
The proposed room-temperature polycrystal comparison cannot test the target's temperature-dependent inertial dulling, MSAD scaling, or high-temperature Portevin-Le Chatelier mechanism.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of how lattice-scale heterogeneity might strengthen a concentrated alloy and provides a baseline, measurements, a stated domain, and a falsification rule. It therefore constitutes a plausible alternative rather than an exact or partial reconstruction. However, it misses nearly all defining elements of the target: oriented FCC single crystals, composition-series comparisons, temperature-dependent CRSS, strain-rate jumps, cryogenic dislocation inertia, and Mn/Fe-dependent high-temperature solute pinning. Its only substantive mechanistic overlap is the general claim that lattice distortion creates resistance to dislocation glide. The proposed causal comparison is weak because cold work necessarily changes dislocation density and organization, while annealing used to remove those confounders can also erase residual strain. E2 supports heterogeneous-strain strengthening in compositionally complex crystals only at a general level, and E1 concerns local chemical order in NiCoCr; neither excerpt supports the specified processing route, alloy-specific claim, or 20% effect. The arbitrary 20% falsification cutoff could also reject a real but smaller causal contribution.
